topic: Irony of Choice : Greater Choice Increases Unhappiness
passage: Shoppers confronting with the choice of thirty different varieties of gourmet chocolates is more likely to walk away without buying any, comparing with when they present with only half a dozen choices.
If employees give a free trip to Paris, they are happy.
If you give them a free trip to Hawaii, they are happy.
[연결사] if you offer them the choice between the two destinations, they are more happy, [=] no matter what they choose.
Why might choice be so disruptive?
The reason is that choice forces us making comparisons and acknowledges absolute disadvantages.
People who choose Paris complains that it doesn't have the ocean and those who choose Hawaii regrets that it doesn't have the museums.
Psychologist Barry Schwartz calls this the 'tyranny of choice' because of rather than providing freedom, it actually constrains our decision-making.

He argues that greater choice decreases unhappiness because we worry that we are going to make the wrong decision and so we get stressing about trying to process all the comparisons in an effort to get it right.
This both decreases our fear of making the wrong choice and lowers expectations which we should be able to get the best choice.
Making the choice, we then start to regret, wondered that it was the right one.
